claim: ZDHHC14 is the only PAT predicted to bind Type-I PDZ domain-containing proteins.
source: The palmitoyl acyltransferase (PAT) ZDHHC14 is highly expressed in the hippocampus and is the only PAT predicted to bind Type-I PDZ domain-containing proteins.
evidence: Based on sequence analysis and prediction of PDZ-binding motifs

claim: PSD93 is a direct ZDHHC14 interactor.
source: Here, we identify the PDZ domain-containing Membrane-associated Guanylate Kinase (MaGUK) PSD93 as a direct ZDHHC14 interactor and substrate.
evidence: Supported by yeast two-hybrid screening and GST pulldown experiments shown in Figure 1

claim: PSD93 is a substrate of ZDHHC14.
source: Here, we identify the PDZ domain-containing Membrane-associated Guanylate Kinase (MaGUK) PSD93 as a direct ZDHHC14 interactor and substrate.
evidence: Supported by ABE assays showing ZDHHC14-dependent palmitoylation of PSD93 in Figure 1C-E

claim: PSD93 localizes to the axon initial segment (AIS).
source: PSD93, but not other MaGUKs, localizes to the axon initial segment (AIS).
evidence: Supported by immunocytochemistry data in Figure 3 and prior literature (Ogawa et al., 2008)

claim: ZDHHC14 controls palmitoylation of PSD93.
source: Using lentiviral-mediated shRNA knockdown in rat hippocampal neurons, we find that ZDHHC14 controls palmitoylation and AIS clustering of PSD93
evidence: Supported by ABE assays in Figure 2C-D showing reduced PSD93 palmitoylation after Zdhhc14 knockdown

claim: ZDHHC14 controls AIS clustering of PSD93.
source: Using lentiviral-mediated shRNA knockdown in rat hippocampal neurons, we find that ZDHHC14 controls palmitoylation and AIS clustering of PSD93
evidence: Supported by immunocytochemistry data in Figure 3 showing reduced PSD93 AIS targeting after Zdhhc14 knockdown

claim: ZDHHC14 controls AIS clustering of Kv1 potassium channels.
source: Using lentiviral-mediated shRNA knockdown in rat hippocampal neurons, we find that ZDHHC14 controls palmitoylation and AIS clustering of PSD93 and also of Kv1 potassium channels, which directly bind PSD93.
evidence: Supported by immunocytochemistry data in Figure 7 showing reduced Kv1 channel AIS targeting after Zdhhc14 knockdown

claim: Kv1 potassium channels directly bind PSD93.
source: Using lentiviral-mediated shRNA knockdown in rat hippocampal neurons, we find that ZDHHC14 controls palmitoylation and AIS clustering of PSD93 and also of Kv1 potassium channels, which directly bind PSD93.
evidence: Supported by prior literature (Kim et al., 1995; Kim et al., 1996)

claim: Neurodevelopmental expression of ZDHHC14 mirrors that of PSD93 and Kv1 channels.
source: Neurodevelopmental expression of ZDHHC14 mirrors that of PSD93 and Kv1 channels
evidence: Supported by western blot data in Figure 5 showing coordinated developmental upregulation

claim: Loss of ZDHHC14 decreases outward currents in hippocampal neurons.
source: consistent with ZDHHC14's importance for Kv1 channel clustering, loss of ZDHHC14 decreases outward currents and increases action potential firing in hippocampal neurons.
evidence: Supported by electrophysiology data in Figure 9A-C

claim: Loss of ZDHHC14 increases action potential firing in hippocampal neurons.
source: consistent with ZDHHC14's importance for Kv1 channel clustering, loss of ZDHHC14 decreases outward currents and increases action potential firing in hippocampal neurons.
evidence: Supported by electrophysiology data in Figure 9D-G

claim: ZDHHC14 is the only PAT with a C-terminal Type-I PDZ ligand (LSSV).
source: However, only the sequence of ZDHHC14 terminates in a Type-I PDZ ligand (LSSV [Leu-Ser-Ser-Val-COOH]; Figure 1A).
evidence: Supported by sequence analysis shown in Figure 1A and Figure 1—figure supplement 1

claim: The LSSV sequence of ZDHHC14 is perfectly conserved in vertebrates.
source: This LSSV sequence is perfectly conserved in vertebrates (Figure 1—figure supplement 1A,B)
evidence: Supported by sequence alignment in Figure 1—figure supplement 1B

claim: Three unique yeast two-hybrid hits encompassed the third PDZ domain (PDZ3) of PSD93.
source: Three unique 'hits' encompassed the third PDZ domain (PDZ3) of the scaffold protein PSD93 (Figure 1—figure supplement 2A).
evidence: Supported by yeast two-hybrid screening results shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2A

claim: PSD93-PDZ3 directly binds the wild type (LSSV) C-terminus of ZDHHC14.
source: Back-transformation experiments using a shorter 'prey' plasmid expressing PSD93-PDZ3 alone revealed that PSD93-PDZ3 directly bound the wild type (LSSV) C-terminus of ZDHHC14 but did not bind a mutant ZDHHC14 C-terminus with a mutated PDZ ligand (LSSE: Figure 1—figure supplement 2B).
evidence: Supported by yeast two-hybrid back-transformation experiments in Figure 1—figure supplement 2B

claim: PSD93-PDZ3 does not bind a mutant ZDHHC14 C-terminus with a mutated PDZ ligand (LSSE).
source: Back-transformation experiments using a shorter 'prey' plasmid expressing PSD93-PDZ3 alone revealed that PSD93-PDZ3 directly bound the wild type (LSSV) C-terminus of ZDHHC14 but did not bind a mutant ZDHHC14 C-terminus with a mutated PDZ ligand (LSSE: Figure 1—figure supplement 2B).
evidence: Supported by yeast two-hybrid back-transformation experiments in Figure 1—figure supplement 2B

claim: GST-ZDHHC14-LSSV (wt) robustly binds PSD93α and PSD93β in lysates of co-transfected HEK293T cells.
source: A glutathione-S-transferase (GST) fusion of the initial ZDHHC14 bait (GST-ZDHHC14-LSSV [wt], abbreviated as GST-14-LSSV (wt) on Figure) robustly bound each of two previously reported palmitoylated PSD93 isoforms, α and β (Brenman et al., 1996; El-Husseini et al., 2000a) in lysates of co-transfected HEK293T cells (Figure 1B).
evidence: Supported by GST pulldown experiments in Figure 1B

claim: Neither PSD93α nor PSD93β binds GST-ZDHHC14-LSSE.
source: In contrast, neither PSD93 isoform bound a GST fusion of ZDHHC14 carrying a mutated PDZ ligand (GST-ZDHHC14-LSSE (GST-14-LSSE on figure); Figure 1B).
evidence: Supported by GST pulldown experiments in Figure 1B

claim: HA-ZDHHC14 robustly increases palmitoylation of both PSD93α and PSD93β in HEK293T cells.
source: However, HA-ZDHHC14 robustly increased palmitoylation of both PSD93 isoforms, with PSD93β palmitoylation increased to a much greater extent than that of PSD93α (Figure 1C [lane 2 versus 5], D, E, and Figure 1—figure supplement 3).
evidence: Supported by ABE assays in Figure 1C-E

claim: PSD93β palmitoylation is increased to a much greater extent than PSD93α by HA-ZDHHC14.
source: However, HA-ZDHHC14 robustly increased palmitoylation of both PSD93 isoforms, with PSD93β palmitoylation increased to a much greater extent than that of PSD93α (Figure 1C [lane 2 versus 5], D, E, and Figure 1—figure supplement 3).
evidence: Supported by ABE assays in Figure 1C-E

claim: HA-ZDHHC14-LSSE palmitoylates both PSD93 isoforms less effectively than wild type HA-ZDHHC14.
source: Interestingly, the HA-ZDHHC14-LSSE mutant (HA-14 LSSE on figure) palmitoylated both PSD93 isoforms less effectively than did wild type HA-ZDHHC14 (Figure 1C [lanes 2 versus 3 and 5 versus 6], D, E, and Figure 1—figure supplement 3).
evidence: Supported by ABE assays in Figure 1C-E

claim: The LSSV PDZ ligand is important for ZDHHC14 to recognize PSD93 as a substrate.
source: This finding suggests that the LSSV PDZ ligand is important, not only for ZDHHC14 to bind PSD93, but also to recognize it as a substrate.
evidence: Inferred from the reduced palmitoylation by LSSE mutant shown in Figure 1C-E

claim: Zdhhc14 sh#1 achieves robust knockdown of ZDHHC14 protein (>90%) one week after infection.
source: Robust knockdown of ZDHHC14 protein was achieved one week after infection (>90%; Figure 2A,B)
evidence: Supported by western blot data in Figure 2A,B

claim: PSD93 palmitoylation is decreased by >60% in Zdhhc14 knockdown cultures.
source: PSD93 was readily detected in ABE samples and its palmitoylation was decreased by >60% in Zdhhc14 'knockdown' cultures (Figure 2C,D).
evidence: Supported by ABE assays in Figure 2C,D

claim: Total levels of PSD93 are decreased after Zdhhc14 knockdown, but to a far lesser extent than palmitoylation.
source: Total levels of PSD93 were also decreased after Zdhhc14 knockdown, but to a far lesser extent than palmitoylation (Figure 2C,E).
evidence: Supported by western blot data in Figure 2C,E

claim: Palmitoylation and levels of GAP43 are unaffected by Zdhhc14 knockdown.
source: In contrast, palmitoylation and levels of another palmitoyl-protein, GAP43, were unaffected by Zdhhc14 knockdown (Figure 2A,C,D).
evidence: Supported by ABE assays and western blots in Figure 2A,C,D

claim: Zdhhc14 sh#2 greatly decreases ZDHHC14 levels.
source: A second, independent Zdhhc14 shRNA (Zdhhc14 sh#2) also greatly decreased ZDHHC14 levels (Figure 2—figure supplement 1A,B)
evidence: Supported by western blot data in Figure 2—figure supplement 1A,B

claim: Zdhhc14 sh#2 decreases PSD93 palmitoylation.
source: A second, independent Zdhhc14 shRNA (Zdhhc14 sh#2) also greatly decreased ZDHHC14 levels (Figure 2—figure supplement 1A,B) and PSD93 palmitoylation (Figure 2—figure supplement 1C–E)
evidence: Supported by ABE assays in Figure 2—figure supplement 1C-E

claim: Zdhhc14 sh#2 does not affect GAP43 palmitoylation.
source: A second, independent Zdhhc14 shRNA (Zdhhc14 sh#2) also greatly decreased ZDHHC14 levels (Figure 2—figure supplement 1A,B) and PSD93 palmitoylation (Figure 2—figure supplement 1C–E), without affecting GAP43 palmitoylation (Figure 2—figure supplements 1C, D).
evidence: Supported by ABE assays in Figure 2—figure supplement 1C,D

claim: ZDHHC14 is the predominant PAT for PSD93 in hippocampal neurons.
source: These findings suggest that ZDHHC14 is the predominant PAT for PSD93 in hippocampal neurons.
evidence: Inferred from the substantial reduction in PSD93 palmitoylation after Zdhhc14 knockdown shown in Figure 2

claim: PSD93 is readily detected at the AIS using a gentle fixation method.
source: Using this method, PSD93 was readily detected at the AIS, defined by enrichment of the master AIS scaffold protein Ankyrin G (AnkG or ANK3; Figure 3A and Figure 3—figure supplement 1B; Huang and Rasband, 2018; Jenkins and Bennett, 2001; Kordeli et al., 1995).
evidence: Supported by immunocytochemistry data in Figure 3A and Figure 3—figure supplement 1B

claim: PSD93 targeting to the AIS is significantly reduced in Zdhhc14 knockdown neurons.
source: However, PSD93 targeting to the AIS was significantly reduced in Zdhhc14 knockdown neurons (Figure 3B,C [mean gray value]).
evidence: Supported by immunocytochemistry data in Figure 3B,C

claim: AIS length is reduced by approximately 35% in Zdhhc14 knockdown neurons.
source: Interestingly, AIS length was also reduced (by approximately 35%) in Zdhhc14 knockdown neurons (Figure 3D).
evidence: Supported by immunocytochemistry data in Figure 3D

claim: Total AIS-localized PSD93 (integrated density) is even more greatly reduced in Zdhhc14 knockdown neurons when reduced AIS length is taken into account.
source: Taking the reduced AIS length into account revealed an even greater reduction of total AIS-localized PSD93 (integrated density) in Zdhhc14 knockdown neurons (Figure 3E).
evidence: Supported by immunocytochemistry data in Figure 3E

claim: Zdhhc14 shRNA#2 decreases PSD93 AIS targeting.
source: Zdhhc14 shRNA#2 also decreased PSD93 AIS targeting and AIS length (Figure 3—figure supplement 2A–E).
evidence: Supported by immunocytochemistry data in Figure 3—figure supplement 2

claim: Zdhhc14 shRNA#2 decreases AIS length.
source: Zdhhc14 shRNA#2 also decreased PSD93 AIS targeting and AIS length (Figure 3—figure supplement 2A–E).
evidence: Supported by immunocytochemistry data in Figure 3—figure supplement 2

claim: There are five cysteine residues in the N-terminus of PSD93β: C10, C16, C18, C22, and C33.
source: There are five cysteine residues in the N-terminus of PSD93β: C10, C16, C18, C22, and C33 (Figure 4—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: Supported by sequence analysis shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1A

claim: ZDHHC14-dependent palmitoylation of full-length PSD93β-myc C16,18S mutant is reduced by only 42%.
source: We found that ZDHHC14-dependent palmitoylation of full-length PSD93β-myc in which cysteines 16 and 18 were both mutated to non-palmitoylatable serine (C16,18S) was reduced by only 42% (Figure 4—figure supplement 1B,C)
evidence: Supported by ABE assays in Figure 4—figure supplement 1B,C

claim: Mutation of C10 to serine (C10S) reduces ZDHHC14-dependent palmitoylation of PSD93β by 88%.
source: Consistent with this notion, mutation of C10 to serine (C10S) reduced ZDHHC14-dependent palmitoylation of PSD93β by 88% (Figure 4—figure supplement 1B,C).
evidence: Supported by ABE assays in Figure 4—figure supplement 1B,C

claim: ZDHHC14-dependent palmitoylation is not completely blocked until all five N-terminal cysteine residues of PSD93β are mutated (5CS mutant).
source: However, ZDHHC14–dependent palmitoylation was not completely blocked until all five N-terminal cysteine residues of PSD93β were mutated (Figure 4—figure supplement 1B,C; '5CS' mutant)
evidence: Supported by ABE assays in Figure 4—figure supplement 1B,C

claim: Each of the five N-terminal cysteine residues of PSD93β can be palmitoylated by ZDHHC14.
source: However, ZDHHC14–dependent palmitoylation was not completely blocked until all five N-terminal cysteine residues of PSD93β were mutated (Figure 4—figure supplement 1B,C; '5CS' mutant), suggesting that each of these sites can be palmitoylated by ZDHHC14.
evidence: Inferred from the ABE assay results in Figure 4—figure supplement 1B,C

claim: Both wtPSD93β-myc and PSD93β−5CS-myc are targeted to punctate structures in dendrites, which are likely synapses.
source: Both wtPSD93β-myc and PSD93β−5CS-myc were targeted to punctate structures in dendrites (Figure 4A,B, respectively), which are likely synapses, in agreement with previous findings (Firestein et al., 2000).
evidence: Supported by immunocytochemistry data in Figure 4A,B and prior literature (Firestein et al., 2000)

claim: wtPSD93β-myc is enriched at the AIS within the axon.
source: However, within the axon, wtPSD93β-myc was enriched at the AIS (Figure 4A)
evidence: Supported by immunocytochemistry data in Figure 4A

claim: PSD93β−5CS-myc is more diffusely distributed within the axon, extending past the AIS.
source: However, within the axon, wtPSD93β-myc was enriched at the AIS (Figure 4A) but PSD93β−5CS-myc was more diffusely distributed, extending past the AIS (Figure 4B).
evidence: Supported by immunocytochemistry data in Figure 4B

claim: wtPSD93β-myc is AIS-enriched in 67+/- 5.77% (SD) of transfected neurons.
source: When PSD93β axonal distribution was scored as AIS-enriched or diffuse, wtPSD93β-myc was AIS-enriched in 67+/- 5.77% (SD) of transfected neurons
evidence: Supported by quantification of immunocytochemistry data in Figure 4C

claim: PSD93β−5CS-myc is AIS-enriched in only 33%+/- 5.77% (SD) of transfected neurons.
source: When PSD93β axonal distribution was scored as AIS-enriched or diffuse, wtPSD93β-myc was AIS-enriched in 67+/- 5.77% (SD) of transfected neurons whereas PSD93β−5CS-myc was AIS-enriched in only 33%+/- 5.77% (SD) of transfected neurons (Figure 4C).
evidence: Supported by quantification of immunocytochemistry data in Figure 4C

claim: Direct palmitoylation is important, although not essential, for PSD93β targeting to the AIS.
source: These findings suggest that direct palmitoylation is important, although not essential, for PSD93β targeting to the AIS.
evidence: Inferred from the partial reduction in AIS targeting of the 5CS mutant shown in Figure 4

claim: The Kv1 channel subunits found at the AIS in hippocampal neurons are Kv1.1, Kv1.2, and Kv1.4.
source: The Kv1 channel subunits found at the AIS in hippocampal neurons are Kv1.1, Kv1.2, and Kv1.4 (Kole et al., 2007; Ogawa et al., 2008)
evidence: Supported by prior literature (Kole et al., 2007; Ogawa et al., 2008)

claim: Kv1.1 is palmitoylated when expressed in non-neuronal cells.
source: Interestingly, Kv1.1 was reported to be palmitoylated when expressed in non-neuronal cells (Gubitosi-Klug et al., 2005).
evidence: Supported by prior literature (Gubitosi-Klug et al., 2005)

claim: The region surrounding the Kv1.1 palmitoyl-cysteine is highly conserved in Kv1.1 orthologs.
source: We realized that the region surrounding the Kv1.1 palmitoyl-cysteine mapped in this prior study is highly conserved in Kv1.1 orthologs, and a homologous cysteine is present in both Kv1.2 and Kv1.4 (Figure 5—figure supplement 1A,B).
evidence: Supported by sequence alignment in Figure 5—figure supplement 1A,B

claim: A homologous cysteine to the Kv1.1 palmitoyl-cysteine is present in both Kv1.2 and Kv1.4.
source: We realized that the region surrounding the Kv1.1 palmitoyl-cysteine mapped in this prior study is highly conserved in Kv1.1 orthologs, and a homologous cysteine is present in both Kv1.2 and Kv1.4 (Figure 5—figure supplement 1A,B).
evidence: Supported by sequence alignment in Figure 5—figure supplement 1A,B

claim: The developmental profiles of ZDHHC14, PSD93, Kv1.1, Kv1.2, and Kv1.4 are almost identical, with each first detectable at DIV8 and steadily increasing to DIV16.
source: Strikingly, the developmental profiles of all five of these proteins were almost identical, with each first detectable at DIV8 and steadily increasing to DIV16 (Figure 5A,B).
evidence: Supported by western blot data in Figure 5A,B

claim: Expression of the GLUN2B subunit of the NMDA receptor is already detected at DIV4 and peaks at DIV12.
source: In contrast, expression of the GLUN2B subunit of the synaptic N-methyl-D-aspartate (NMDA) glutamate receptor was already detected at DIV4 and peaked at DIV12 (Figure 5A,B).
evidence: Supported by western blot data in Figure 5A,B

claim: Coordinated developmental upregulation of ZDHHC14 with PSD93 and Kv1 channels is consistent with a shared function in hippocampal neurons.
source: This coordinated developmental upregulation of ZDHHC14 with PSD93 and Kv1 channels is consistent with a shared function in hippocampal neurons.
evidence: Inferred from the developmental expression data in Figure 5

claim: Zdhhc14 knockdown reduces palmitoylation of Kv1.1 by 35%.
source: Consistent with our hypothesis, Zdhhc14 knockdown reduced palmitoylation of Kv1.1, Kv1.2, and Kv1.4 by 35, 31, and 65%, respectively (Figure 6A,B).
evidence: Supported by ABE assays in Figure 6A,B

claim: Zdhhc14 knockdown reduces palmitoylation of Kv1.2 by 31%.
source: Consistent with our hypothesis, Zdhhc14 knockdown reduced palmitoylation of Kv1.1, Kv1.2, and Kv1.4 by 35, 31, and 65%, respectively (Figure 6A,B).
evidence: Supported by ABE assays in Figure 6A,B

claim: Zdhhc14 knockdown reduces palmitoylation of Kv1.4 by 65%.
source: Consistent with our hypothesis, Zdhhc14 knockdown reduced palmitoylation of Kv1.1, Kv1.2, and Kv1.4 by 35, 31, and 65%, respectively (Figure 6A,B).
evidence: Supported by ABE assays in Figure 6A,B

claim: Zdhhc14 knockdown reduces total levels of Kv1.2 and Kv1.4, but to a lesser extent than palmitoylation.
source: Zdhhc14 knockdown also reduced total levels of Kv1.2 and Kv1.4, but to a lesser extent than palmitoylation (Figure 6A,C).
evidence: Supported by western blot data in Figure 6A,C

claim: ZDHHC14 is a PAT for Kv1 channels in hippocampal neurons.
source: These findings suggest that ZDHHC14 is a PAT for Kv1 channels in hippocampal neurons.
evidence: Inferred from the reduced Kv1 channel palmitoylation after Zdhhc14 knockdown shown in Figure 6

claim: All three Kv1 channels (Kv1.1, Kv1.2, Kv1.4) are readily detected at the AIS in neurons infected with control lentivirus.
source: All three Kv1 channels were readily detected at the AIS in neurons infected with control lentivirus (Figure 7A,E,I).
evidence: Supported by immunocytochemistry data in Figure 7A,E,I

claim: AIS targeting of Kv1.1 is reduced in Zdhhc14 knockdown neurons.
source: However, in Zdhhc14 knockdown neurons, AIS targeting of Kv1.1 (Figure 7B,C,D), Kv1.2 (Figure 7F,G,H), and Kv1.4 (Figure 7J,K,L) was reduced.
evidence: Supported by immunocytochemistry data in Figure 7B,C,D

claim: AIS targeting of Kv1.2 is reduced in Zdhhc14 knockdown neurons.
source: However, in Zdhhc14 knockdown neurons, AIS targeting of Kv1.1 (Figure 7B,C,D), Kv1.2 (Figure 7F,G,H), and Kv1.4 (Figure 7J,K,L) was reduced.
evidence: Supported by immunocytochemistry data in Figure 7F,G,H

claim: AIS targeting of Kv1.4 is reduced in Zdhhc14 knockdown neurons.
source: However, in Zdhhc14 knockdown neurons, AIS targeting of Kv1.1 (Figure 7B,C,D), Kv1.2 (Figure 7F,G,H), and Kv1.4 (Figure 7J,K,L) was reduced.
evidence: Supported by immunocytochemistry data in Figure 7J,K,L

claim: The total amount of AIS-localized Kv1.2 is significantly reduced in Zdhhc14 knockdown neurons.
source: We note that the total amount of AIS-localized Kv1.2 was significantly reduced, even though the reduction in Kv1.2 mean intensity at the AIS did not reach statistical significance (Figure 7G,H).
evidence: Supported by immunocytochemistry data in Figure 7G,H

claim: ZDHHC14 is required for AIS targeting of Kv1 channel subunits.
source: These findings suggest that ZDHHC14 is required for AIS targeting of Kv1 channel subunits.
evidence: Inferred from the reduced Kv1 channel AIS targeting after Zdhhc14 knockdown shown in Figure 7

claim: HA-ZDHHC14 localizes predominantly to the somatic Golgi and to punctate structures in dendrites.
source: Interestingly, we found that HA-ZDHHC14 localized predominantly to the somatic Golgi and to punctate structures in dendrites (Figure 8A–C).
evidence: Supported by immunocytochemistry data in Figure 8A-C

claim: ZDHHC14 is detectable in axons but does not enrich at the AIS.
source: ZDHHC14 was also detectable in axons but did not enrich at the AIS (Figure 8C).
evidence: Supported by immunocytochemistry data in Figure 8C

claim: ZDHHC14-dependent palmitoylation of PSD93 and Kv1 channels likely occurs within the Golgi, rather than directly at the AIS.
source: These findings increase the likelihood that ZDHHC14-dependent palmitoylation of PSD93 and Kv1 channels occurs within the Golgi, rather than directly at the AIS.
evidence: Inferred from the Golgi localization of ZDHHC14 shown in Figure 8

claim: The density of outward currents is dramatically decreased in Zdhhc14 knockdown neurons.
source: Indeed, we found that the density of outward currents, which are likely mediated by voltage-dependent potassium channels, was dramatically decreased in Zdhhc14 knockdown neurons (Figure 9A–C).
evidence: Supported by electrophysiology data in Figure 9A-C

claim: Zdhhc14 knockdown neurons fire a markedly greater number of action potentials in response to injection of a given current.
source: Consistent with a reduced Kv1 number and/or function, Zdhhc14 knockdown neurons fired a markedly greater number of APs in response to injection of a given current (Figure 9D–F).
evidence: Supported by electrophysiology data in Figure 9D-F

claim: The latency to the first action potential is decreased in Zdhhc14 knockdown neurons.
source: Moreover, the latency to the first action potential, rheobase (the minimum current required to generate an AP), and the rate of AP repolarization were all decreased in Zdhhc14 knockdown neurons (Figure 9D–E,G, Table 1).
evidence: Supported by electrophysiology data in Figure 9D-E,G and Table 1

claim: Rheobase is decreased in Zdhhc14 knockdown neurons.
source: Moreover, the latency to the first action potential, rheobase (the minimum current required to generate an AP), and the rate of AP repolarization were all decreased in Zdhhc14 knockdown neurons (Figure 9D–E,G, Table 1).
evidence: Supported by electrophysiology data in Table 1

claim: The rate of action potential repolarization is decreased in Zdhhc14 knockdown neurons.
source: Moreover, the latency to the first action potential, rheobase (the minimum current required to generate an AP), and the rate of AP repolarization were all decreased in Zdhhc14 knockdown neurons (Figure 9D–E,G, Table 1).
evidence: Supported by electrophysiology data in Table 1

claim: The overall increased excitability and individual changes in action potential properties are consistent with a loss of AIS-localized Kv1 channels in the absence of ZDHHC14.
source: The overall increased excitability and the individual changes in AP properties are all consistent with a loss of AIS-localized Kv1 channels in the absence of ZDHHC14.
evidence: Inferred from the electrophysiology data in Figure 9 and Table 1, and known roles of Kv1 channels

claim: Input resistance is slightly increased in Zdhhc14 knockdown neurons.
source: We also observed a slightly increased input resistance and a slightly depolarized resting membrane potential in Zdhhc14 knockdown neurons (Table 1).
evidence: Supported by electrophysiology data in Table 1

claim: Resting membrane potential is slightly depolarized in Zdhhc14 knockdown neurons.
source: We also observed a slightly increased input resistance and a slightly depolarized resting membrane potential in Zdhhc14 knockdown neurons (Table 1).
evidence: Supported by electrophysiology data in Table 1

claim: Palmitoylation plays key roles in neurons, particularly at synapses where many scaffold proteins and ion channels and receptors are palmitoylated.
source: Palmitoylation plays key roles in neurons (Sanders et al., 2015), particularly at synapses where many scaffold proteins and ion channels and receptors are palmitoylated (Matt et al., 2019; Naumenko and Ponimaskin, 2018; Thomas and Huganir, 2013b).
evidence: Supported by citations to published literature

claim: ZDHHC14 may be the most highly expressed PAT in the hippocampus.
source: The lack of investigation of ZDHHC14 is perhaps surprising, given that this PAT is highly expressed in the hippocampus (Cembrowski et al., 2016; Zeisel et al., 2018) and may even be the most highly expressed PAT in this brain region (Cajigas et al., 2012).
evidence: Supported by citation to published literature (Cajigas et al., 2012)

claim: ZDHHC14 is one of only four PATs intolerant to loss of function genetic mutations in humans.
source: ZDHHC14 is also one of only four PATs intolerant to loss of function genetic mutations in humans (Lek et al., 2016).
evidence: Supported by citation to published literature (Lek et al., 2016)

claim: Role(s) of ZDHHC14 cannot be compensated for by other PATs.
source: This latter finding suggests that role(s) of ZDHHC14 cannot be compensated for by other PATs, which might be explained by ZDHHC14's unique predicted PDZ-binding ability.
evidence: Inferred from the intolerance to loss of function mutations

claim: PSD93 is a known palmitoyl-protein.
source: Like its close paralog, PSD95, PSD93 is a known palmitoyl-protein (El-Husseini et al., 2000b; Topinka and Bredt, 1998).
evidence: Supported by citations to published literature (El-Husseini et al., 2000b; Topinka and Bredt, 1998)

claim: Palmitoylation controls PSD95 targeting to the post-synaptic membrane.
source: However, while palmitoylation is well described to control PSD95 targeting to the post-synaptic membrane (Firestein et al., 2000), the role of PSD93 palmitoylation is less clear.
evidence: Supported by citation to published literature (Firestein et al., 2000)

claim: Clustering of Kv1 channels at the AIS was previously reported to be PSD93-dependent.
source: Loss of ZDHHC14 also reduces palmitoylation and AIS targeting of Kv1 family potassium channels, whose clustering at the AIS was previously reported to be PSD93-dependent (Ogawa et al., 2008).
evidence: Supported by citation to published literature (Ogawa et al., 2008)

claim: Kv1 channels play a role in constraining action potential firing.
source: Consistent with this model, and with the known role of Kv1 channels in constraining action potential firing (Yamada and Kuba, 2016), loss of ZDHHC14 reduces outward currents, which are likely mediated by voltage-dependent potassium channels, and also increases neuronal excitability.
evidence: Supported by citation to published literature (Yamada and Kuba, 2016)

claim: Voltage-gated calcium channels and neurotransmitter receptors must be clustered pre- and post-synaptically to ensure the fidelity of synaptic transmission.
source: For example, voltage-gated calcium channels and neurotransmitter receptors must be clustered pre- and post-synaptically, respectively, to ensure the fidelity of synaptic transmission (Buonarati et al., 2019; Dolphin and Lee, 2020; Sanz-Clemente et al., 2013; Suh et al., 2018).
evidence: Supported by citations to published literature

claim: Voltage-gated sodium and potassium channels must be clustered at the axon initial segment (AIS) and at or near nodes of Ranvier to ensure correct initiation and propagation of action potentials.
source: In addition, voltage-gated sodium and potassium channels must be clustered at the axon initial segment (AIS) and, in myelinated axons, at or near nodes of Ranvier, to ensure correct initiation and propagation of action potentials (Catterall, 1981; Huang and Rasband, 2018; Leterrier, 2018; Lorincz and Nusser, 2008; Nelson and Jenkins, 2017; Waxman and Foster, 1980).
evidence: Supported by citations to published literature

claim: Non-enzymatic scaffold proteins, particularly those containing PDZ domains, directly bind the intracellular C-terminal tails of several families of receptors and channels and control their trafficking and/or stability at precise subcellular sites.
source: In particular, non-enzymatic scaffold proteins, particularly those containing PSD95/discs large/ZO-1 (PDZ) domains, directly bind the intracellular C-terminal tails of several families of receptors and channels and thereby control their trafficking to, and/or stability at, precise subcellular sites (Kim and Sheng, 2004).
evidence: Supported by citation to published literature (Kim and Sheng, 2004)

claim: Type-I PDZ domains bind C-terminal sequences ending in S/T-X-V.
source: PDZ domains are subdivided into several classes with the two best known subclasses, Type-I and Type-II PDZ domains, binding C-terminal sequences ending in S/T-X-V (where X is any amino acid) and Φ-X-Φ (where Φ is a hydrophobic amino acid), respectively (Nourry et al., 2003).
evidence: Supported by citation to published literature (Nourry et al., 2003)

claim: Type-II PDZ domains bind C-terminal sequences ending in Φ-X-Φ (where Φ is a hydrophobic amino acid).
source: PDZ domains are subdivided into several classes with the two best known subclasses, Type-I and Type-II PDZ domains, binding C-terminal sequences ending in S/T-X-V (where X is any amino acid) and Φ-X-Φ (where Φ is a hydrophobic amino acid), respectively (Nourry et al., 2003).
evidence: Supported by citation to published literature (Nourry et al., 2003)

claim: Many PATs possess C-terminal sequences that are predicted to bind PDZ domain proteins.
source: We previously suggested that these two mechanisms might act in concert because a surprising number of palmitoyl acyltransferases (PATs) possess C-terminal sequences that are themselves predicted to bind PDZ domain proteins (Thomas and Hayashi, 2013a).
evidence: Supported by citation to published literature (Thomas and Hayashi, 2013a)

claim: Seven of 24 mouse PATs have sequences that terminate in a predicted PDZ ligand.
source: Seven of 24 mouse and eight of 23 human PATs have sequences that terminate in a predicted PDZ ligand (Thomas and Hayashi, 2013a).
evidence: Supported by citation to published literature (Thomas and Hayashi, 2013a)

claim: Eight of 23 human PATs have sequences that terminate in a predicted PDZ ligand.
source: Seven of 24 mouse and eight of 23 human PATs have sequences that terminate in a predicted PDZ ligand (Thomas and Hayashi, 2013a).
evidence: Supported by citation to published literature (Thomas and Hayashi, 2013a)

claim: PSD93 and PSD95 are close paralogs.
source: Like its close paralog, PSD95, PSD93 is a known palmitoyl-protein (El-Husseini et al., 2000b; Topinka and Bredt, 1998).
evidence: Based on established scientific knowledge of protein families

claim: PSD93 was previously reported to be the only MaGUK that also clusters at the AIS.
source: Interestingly, PSD93 was previously reported to be the only MaGUK that also clusters at the AIS (Ogawa et al., 2008)
evidence: Supported by citation to published literature (Ogawa et al., 2008)

claim: Kv1 clustering by PSD93 likely involves binding of Kv1.1/1.2/1.4 C-termini to PSD93's second PDZ domain.
source: prior work from non-neuronal cells suggested that Kv1 clustering by PSD93 likely involves binding of Kv1.1/1.2/1.4 C-termini, each of which terminates in a Type-I PDZ ligand, to PSD93's second PDZ domain (Kim et al., 1996; Kim et al., 1995).
evidence: Supported by citations to published literature (Kim et al., 1996; Kim et al., 1995)

claim: Each of Kv1.1, Kv1.2, and Kv1.4 C-termini terminates in a Type-I PDZ ligand.
source: prior work from non-neuronal cells suggested that Kv1 clustering by PSD93 likely involves binding of Kv1.1/1.2/1.4 C-termini, each of which terminates in a Type-I PDZ ligand, to PSD93's second PDZ domain (Kim et al., 1996; Kim et al., 1995).
evidence: Supported by sequence analysis in Figure 5—figure supplement 1B and citations

claim: Decreased AIS length is a well-known homeostatic response to increased neuronal excitability.
source: The decreased AIS length after loss of ZDHHC14 (Figure 3D) is consistent with this notion, because decreased AIS length is a well-known homeostatic response to increased neuronal excitability (Dumitrescu et al., 2016; Grubb and Burrone, 2010; Grubb et al., 2011)
evidence: Supported by citations to published literature (Dumitrescu et al., 2016; Grubb and Burrone, 2010; Grubb et al., 2011)

claim: PSD93 was reported to be predominantly palmitoylated at C16 and C18 in a prior study using a truncated PSD93β cDNA.
source: PSD93β was reported to be predominantly palmitoylated at C16 and C18, but this prior study Firestein et al., 2000 used a truncated PSD93β cDNA lacking C10 and additional N-terminal sequences now ascribed to PSD93 (Rattus norvegicus XP_017445141.1, Homo sapiens NP_001338205.1).
evidence: Supported by citation to published literature (Firestein et al., 2000)

claim: Palmitoylation was reported to be dispensable for PSD93 targeting to synapses.
source: Although our results strongly suggested that ZDHHC14 controls PSD93 palmitoylation in neurons, this modification was reported to be dispensable for PSD93 targeting to synapses (Firestein et al., 2000).
evidence: Supported by citation to published literature (Firestein et al., 2000)

claim: PSD93 is readily detected at presumptive synapses using standard fixation conditions.
source: Consistent with prior findings, we robustly detected PSD93 at presumptive synapses (Firestein et al., 2000; Kim et al., 1996) and at the AIS (Ogawa et al., 2008; Figure 3—figure supplement 1A) in hippocampal neurons using standard fixation conditions.
evidence: Supported by immunocytochemistry data in Figure 3—figure supplement 1A and citations

claim: A gentle fixation method preferentially reveals the AIS-localized pool of PSD93.
source: However, for our investigations of the importance of ZDHHC14, we used a previously described gentle fixation method, which preferentially reveals the AIS-localized pool of PSD93 (Ogawa et al., 2008; Figure 3—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: Supported by immunocytochemistry data in Figure 3—figure supplement 1B and citation to published literature (Ogawa et al., 2008)

claim: Ankyrin G (AnkG or ANK3) is the master AIS scaffold protein.
source: Using this method, PSD93 was readily detected at the AIS, defined by enrichment of the master AIS scaffold protein Ankyrin G (AnkG or ANK3; Figure 3A and Figure 3—figure supplement 1B; Huang and Rasband, 2018; Jenkins and Bennett, 2001; Kordeli et al., 1995).
evidence: Supported by citations to published literature (Huang and Rasband, 2018; Jenkins and Bennett, 2001; Kordeli et al., 1995)

claim: Palmitoylation within the Golgi was reported to facilitate forward trafficking of the BK potassium channel.
source: This mechanism is not unprecedented, as palmitoylation within the Golgi was reported to facilitate forward trafficking of the BK potassium channel (Tian et al., 2012).
evidence: Supported by citation to published literature (Tian et al., 2012)

claim: The zebrafish ortholog of Kv1.1 can be palmitoylated by the PAT HIP14 (ZDHHC17) in cotransfected HEK293 cells.
source: Some potential insight into this issue is provided by a recent report that the zebrafish ortholog of Kv1.1 could be palmitoylated by the PAT HIP14 (ZDHHC17) in cotransfected HEK293 cells, although palmitoylation of endogenous neuronal Kv1.1 by ZDHHC17/HIP14 was not assessed (Nelson et al., 2020).
evidence: Supported by citation to published literature (Nelson et al., 2020)

claim: Loss of ZDHHC17 does not affect PSD93 palmitoylation in mice.
source: However, ZDHHC17 is less likely to mediate residual PSD93 palmitoylation because this PAT lacks a Type-I PDZ ligand and loss of ZDHHC17 does not affect PSD93 palmitoylation in mice (Wan et al., 2013).
evidence: Supported by citation to published literature (Wan et al., 2013)

claim: Kv1.2 is first detectably enriched at the AIS of cultured hippocampal neurons at DIV13.
source: However, a prior study reported, albeit non-quantitatively, that Kv1.2 is first detectably enriched at the AIS of cultured hippocampal neurons at a very similar timepoint (DIV13) to when we observe marked upregulation of total Kv1.2 protein levels (DIV12; Figure 5; Sánchez-Ponce et al., 2012).
evidence: Supported by citation to published literature (Sánchez-Ponce et al., 2012)

claim: Sodium channel clustering in proximal axons is first observed immunohistologically in vertebrates.
source: Intriguing, additional support for a shared function of ZDHHC14, PSD93, and Kv1 channels in AIS regulation emerges from examining the evolutionary conservation of ZDHHC14, PSD93, and the AIS itself. Sodium channel clustering in proximal axons is first observed immunohistologically in vertebrates, coincident with the evolution of AIS-anchoring domains in these channels (Kole and Stuart, 2012).
evidence: Supported by citation to published literature (Kole and Stuart, 2012)

claim: N-terminal palmitoylation sites are only present in vertebrate orthologs of PSD93 and are absent in the fruit fly PSD93 ortholog Discs Large (DLG).
source: Similarly, N-terminal palmitoylation sites are only present in vertebrate orthologs of PSD93 and are absent in the fruit fly PSD93 ortholog Discs Large (DLG) (Thomas and Hayashi, 2013a).
evidence: Supported by citation to published literature (Thomas and Hayashi, 2013a)

claim: ZDHHC14's PDZ ligand is first observed in simple chordates (Ciona intestinalis) and vertebrates.
source: Lastly, ZDHHC14's PDZ ligand, which greatly increases ZDHHC14's ability to palmitoylate PSD93 (Figure 1), is first observed in simple chordates (Ciona intestinalis) and vertebrates (Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Supported by sequence alignment in Figure 1—figure supplement 1

claim: Palmitoyl-sites and PDZ ligands in Kv1 channels are more evolutionarily ancient than those in ZDHHC14 and PSD93.
source: In contrast, palmitoyl-sites and PDZ ligands in Kv1 channels are more evolutionarily ancient (Figure 5—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: Supported by sequence alignment in Figure 5—figure supplement 1B

claim: The ability of ZDHHC14 to palmitoylate PSD93, and for palmitoyl-PSD93 to act as a scaffold to cluster Kv1 channels at the AIS, appear to have evolved with the appearance of the AIS itself.
source: However, the ability of ZDHHC14 to palmitoylate PSD93, and for palmitoyl-PSD93 to act as a scaffold to cluster Kv1 channels at the AIS, appear to have evolved with the appearance of the AIS itself as nervous systems became more complex.
evidence: Inferred from evolutionary conservation analysis and functional data

claim: Kv1-type channels activate at subthreshold membrane potentials and counteract voltage-gated sodium channel (Nav) currents, thereby dampening action potential firing and reducing neuronal excitability.
source: Moreover, Kv1-type channels activate at subthreshold membrane potentials and counteract voltage-gated sodium channel (Nav) currents, thereby dampening action potential firing and reducing neuronal excitability (Clark et al., 2009; Dodson et al., 2002; Yamada and Kuba, 2016).
evidence: Supported by citations to published literature (Clark et al., 2009; Dodson et al., 2002; Yamada and Kuba, 2016)

claim: Kv1-type channels regulate action potential firing by suppressing generation of, as well as shortening, action potentials.
source: For example, Kv1-type channels are known to regulate AP firing by suppressing generation of, as well as shortening, action potentials (Yamada and Kuba, 2016)
evidence: Supported by citation to published literature (Yamada and Kuba, 2016)

claim: Slight AP broadening was observed following acute block of Kv1 channels.
source: Indeed, the slight but significant AP broadening that we observed in Zdhhc14 knockdown neurons (half-width; Table 1) was also seen following acute block of Kv1 channels (Guan et al., 2018; Kole et al., 2007).
evidence: Supported by citations to published literature (Guan et al., 2018; Kole et al., 2007)

claim: Many other AIS-localized ion channels, scaffolds, and cell adhesion molecules are either known or predicted to be palmitoylated.
source: It is especially intriguing that many other AIS-localized ion channels, scaffolds, and cell adhesion molecules are either known or predicted to be palmitoylated (Blanc et al., 2015; He et al., 2012; Nelson and Jenkins, 2017; Pei et al., 2016).
evidence: Supported by citations to published literature (Blanc et al., 2015; He et al., 2012; Nelson and Jenkins, 2017; Pei et al., 2016)

claim: Endogenous PSD93/PSD95 heteromultimers were not detected in brain tissue.
source: However, subsequent studies of endogenous proteins from brain tissue suggested that although both PSD95 and PSD93 are found in multimeric complexes, endogenous PSD93/PSD95 heteromultimers were not detected (i.e. the endogenous multimeric complexes consist of homomeric PSD95 or PSD93, but not both) (Hsueh et al., 1997).
evidence: Supported by citation to published literature (Hsueh et al., 1997)

claim: PSD95 is undetectable at the AIS.
source: We also note that our PSD93 antibody is validated using knockout tissue by the supplier. This antibody might still theoretically detect PSD95 in immunocytochemical experiments, but a prior study reported that PSD95 (detected with another widely used monoclonal antibody, which is itself validated using knockout tissue) is undetectable at the AIS, whereas PSD93 is AIS-localized (Ogawa et al., 2008).
evidence: Supported by citation to published literature (Ogawa et al., 2008)

claim: Palmitoylation modulates voltage-sensing of Kv1.1 expressed in Sf9 cells.
source: Indeed, palmitoylation was previously shown to modulate voltage-sensing of Kv1.1 expressed in Sf9 cells and loss of Kv1.1 palmitoylation decreased current amplitude (Gubitosi-Klug et al., 2005).
evidence: Supported by citation to published literature (Gubitosi-Klug et al., 2005)

claim: Loss of Kv1.1 palmitoylation decreases current amplitude.
source: Indeed, palmitoylation was previously shown to modulate voltage-sensing of Kv1.1 expressed in Sf9 cells and loss of Kv1.1 palmitoylation decreased current amplitude (Gubitosi-Klug et al., 2005).
evidence: Supported by citation to published literature (Gubitosi-Klug et al., 2005)

claim: Mutations in multiple Kv1 channel genes are associated with epilepsy, myokemia, episodic ataxia, schizophrenia, autism spectrum disorder, and intellectual disability.
source: Indeed, mutations in multiple Kv1 channel genes and copy number variations of the Dlg2 gene (which codes for PSD93) are associated with multiple neurological conditions characterized by neuronal hyperexcitability, including epilepsy, myokemia, episodic ataxia, schizophrenia, autism spectrum disorder, and intellectual disability (Cuscó et al., 2009; Eunson et al., 2000; Felix, 2000; Gao et al., 2018; Reggiani et al., 2017; Walsh et al., 2008).
evidence: Supported by citations to published literature

claim: Copy number variations of the Dlg2 gene (which codes for PSD93) are associated with epilepsy, myokemia, episodic ataxia, schizophrenia, autism spectrum disorder, and intellectual disability.
source: Indeed, mutations in multiple Kv1 channel genes and copy number variations of the Dlg2 gene (which codes for PSD93) are associated with multiple neurological conditions characterized by neuronal hyperexcitability, including epilepsy, myokemia, episodic ataxia, schizophrenia, autism spectrum disorder, and intellectual disability (Cuscó et al., 2009; Eunson et al., 2000; Felix, 2000; Gao et al., 2018; Reggiani et al., 2017; Walsh et al., 2008).
evidence: Supported by citations to published literature

claim: ZDHHC14 has not been associated with any neuropathological condition.
source: In contrast, ZDHHC14 has not, thus far, been associated with any neuropathological condition.
evidence: Based on lack of reports in the literature

claim: ZDHHC14 may be an essential gene.
source: However, ZDHHC14 is one of only four PATs intolerant to loss of function mutations in humans, suggesting that it may be an essential gene (Lek et al., 2016).
evidence: Inferred from intolerance to loss of function mutations reported in Lek et al., 2016

claim: ZDHHC14's potential action as a master regulator of AIS structure and function could account for its indispensability.
source: While it is possible that roles of ZDHHC14 in non-neuronal tissues underlie this requirement, it is again intriguing that ZDHHC14's potential action as a master regulator of AIS structure and function could account for its indispensability.
evidence: Speculative reasoning based on the findings of the study

claim: These findings identify the first substrates of ZDHHC14 in any system.
source: To our knowledge, these findings identify the first substrates of ZDHHC14 in any system
evidence: Based on the authors' knowledge of the literature

claim: These findings reveal, for the first time, a role for PSD93 palmitoylation in neurons.
source: To our knowledge, these findings identify the first substrates of ZDHHC14 in any system and reveal, for the first time, a role for PSD93 palmitoylation in neurons, a question that has remained unanswered for two decades.
evidence: Based on the authors' knowledge of the literature

claim: Kv1 family voltage-gated potassium channels are endogenously palmitoylated in neurons.
source: We also demonstrate that Kv1 family voltage-gated potassium channels are endogenously palmitoylated in neurons
evidence: Supported by ABE assays in Figure 6

claim: These findings have important implications for understanding physiological regulation of neuronal excitability and its dysfunction in epilepsy and/or other conditions marked by hyper-excitation.
source: These findings have important implications for our understanding of physiological regulation of neuronal excitability and its dysfunction in epilepsy and/or other conditions marked by hyper-excitation.
evidence: Inferred from the findings of the study and their potential broader significance

claim: ZDHHC5 and ZDHHC8 use their Type-II PDZ ligands to bind and palmitoylate the PDZ domain-containing protein GRIP1b.
source: This PDZ ligand-dependent mechanism of substrate recognition by a PAT was also reported for ZDHHC5 and ZDHHC8, which use their Type-II PDZ ligands to bind and palmitoylate the PDZ domain-containing protein GRIP1b (Thomas et al., 2012).
evidence: Supported by citation to published literature (Thomas et al., 2012)

claim: Certain kinases bind and phosphorylate PDZ domain-containing substrates in a manner dependent on the kinase's PDZ ligand.
source: While these are the only three PATs known to use this mechanism of substrate recognition, certain kinases also bind and phosphorylate PDZ domain-containing substrates in a manner dependent on the kinase's PDZ ligand (Hasegawa et al., 1999; Sabio et al., 2004; Thomas et al., 2005).
evidence: Supported by citations to published literature (Hasegawa et al., 1999; Sabio et al., 2004; Thomas et al., 2005)

claim: The C-termini of Kv1.1, Kv1.2, and Kv1.4 are critically important for their axonal targeting.
source: Although the C-termini of Kv1.1, Kv1.2, and Kv1.4 are not predicted to bind ZDHHC14, they all terminate in Type-I PDZ ligands that (i) are critically important for their axonal targeting (Arnold and Clapham, 1999)
evidence: Supported by citation to published literature (Arnold and Clapham, 1999)

claim: PSD93 and PSD95 were reported to form heteromultimers in transfected non-neuronal cells.
source: Given that ZDHHC14 may regulate other palmitoyl-proteins, it is theoretically possible that signals in our biochemical and/or immunocytochemical experiments could represent heteromultimers of PSD93 and its paralogous palmitoyl-protein PSD95, which were reported in transfected non-neuronal cells (Kim et al., 1996).
evidence: Supported by citation to published literature (Kim et al., 1996)

claim: Mutating the palmitoyl-cysteines of PSD93β reduces AIS localization of PSD93 to a lesser extent than loss of ZDHHC14 itself.
source: We also recognize that mutating the palmitoyl-cysteines of the PSD93β isoform reduces AIS localization of PSD93 (Figure 4) to a lesser extent than is seen following loss of ZDHHC14 itself (Figure 3).
evidence: Supported by comparison of data in Figure 3 and Figure 4

claim: Additional ZDHHC14 substrate(s) may contribute to AIS localization of PSD93.
source: These findings suggest that additional ZDHHC14 substrate(s) may also contribute to AIS localization of PSD93.
evidence: Inferred from the differential effects of palmitoyl-site mutation versus ZDHHC14 loss

claim: The effect of ZDHHC14 loss on neuronal excitability is more dramatic than the effect on AIS targeting of any individual Kv1 channel.
source: We also note that the effect of ZDHHC14 loss on neuronal excitability is more dramatic than the effect on AIS targeting of any individual Kv1 channel (Figure 7 versus 9).
evidence: Supported by comparison of data in Figure 7 and Figure 9

claim: Palmitoylation may regulate Kv1 channel electrophysiological responses in addition to channel targeting to the AIS.
source: One possible explanation for this finding is that palmitoylation not only regulates channel targeting to the AIS but also regulates Kv1 channel electrophysiological responses.
evidence: Speculative reasoning to explain the discrepancy between targeting and excitability effects

claim: ZDHHC14 may be a master regulator of multiple AIS ion channels and/or scaffold proteins.
source: Importantly, though, another intriguing possibility is that ZDHHC14 is a master regulator of multiple AIS ion channels and/or scaffold proteins and that impaired localization and/or function of these additional ZDHHC14 substrates further impacts neuronal excitability.
evidence: Speculative reasoning based on the findings of the study

claim: Dysregulated palmitoylation of PSD93 and/or Kv1 channels may contribute to the pathogenesis of conditions characterized by neuronal hyperexcitability.
source: It is an intriguing possibility that dysregulated palmitoylation of PSD93 and/or Kv1 channels contributes to the pathogenesis of such conditions.
evidence: Speculative reasoning based on the findings of the study and known disease associations

claim: Palmitoylation of PSD93 by ZDHHC14 is important for regulating targeting of voltage-gated ion channels to the AIS.
source: In summary, our findings that palmitoylation of PSD93 by ZDHHC14 is important for regulating targeting of voltage-gated ion channels to the AIS and for neuronal excitability, provide key insights into multiple outstanding questions.
evidence: Supported by the collective data from the study

claim: Palmitoylation of PSD93 by ZDHHC14 is important for neuronal excitability.
source: In summary, our findings that palmitoylation of PSD93 by ZDHHC14 is important for regulating targeting of voltage-gated ion channels to the AIS and for neuronal excitability, provide key insights into multiple outstanding questions.
evidence: Supported by the collective data from the study

claim: These findings provide additional mechanistic insight into the regulation of Kv1 channel AIS targeting and physiology.
source: We also demonstrate that Kv1 family voltage-gated potassium channels are endogenously palmitoylated in neurons and provide additional mechanistic insight into the regulation of their AIS targeting and physiology.
evidence: Supported by the collective data from the study
